A battery cathode near 1,000 Wh/kg that barely swells; hydrogen without iridium; the energy radar.
TECH RADAR
A battery material that packs more energy without wearing itself out
No. 6 · Tuesday 27 October 2026 · Energy · 6 min read
 
IN 30 SECONDS
1US national laboratories tame the most energy-dense common cathode material: it stores 973 Wh per kg and keeps 80% of its capacity after 1,800 cycles in pouch cells.
2A Korean team makes hydrogen electrolysers run without iridium, one of the rarest metals on Earth: over 1,000 hours of operation in a single test cell.
3Energy radar: research is flat and slowing this year, but new battery projects on GitHub more than tripled, while hydrogen projects fell by almost half.

new LLM papers added to the archive today
SIGNAL OF THE DAY
A nickel cathode near 1,000 Wh/kg that hardly changes shape
ACS Energy Letters · 25 October  Journal  High-impact journal
Who wrote it: Yaqi Jing and 13 others · Brookhaven National Laboratory, Argonne National Laboratory (United States) · among the authors Huolin L. Xin, h-index 102
Context. The cathode is the part of a lithium-ion battery that largely decides how much energy it holds. A material made almost only of nickel and lithium (LiNiO2) is close to the practical energy limit, but it shrinks and swells at every charge, cracks and loses capacity quickly; most car batteries therefore add costly cobalt.
The team adds just 5% of a mix of other elements, with no cobalt. The strain on the crystal during charging drops from 7.4% to 2.1%, so it barely changes shape. The material stores 258 mAh per gram and 973 Wh per kg, keeps 80% of its capacity after 1,800 cycles in pouch cells and is more stable when heated. It is today's signal because it tackles the main weakness of the most energy-dense cathode without losing energy or using cobalt.
PAPERS OF THE DAY · ENERGY
Catalysts for clean energystable
Research share +3% in 3 years · 15,706 papers in 2025
What it is about. Catalysts speed up chemical reactions without being used up. In energy they are needed above all to split water into hydrogen and oxygen with electricity, in electrolysers.
Stabilizing Cobalt Sites with d10-Configured p-Block Cations for Iridium-Free Proton Exchange Membrane Water Electrolysis
ACS Catalysis · 24 October  Journal  High-impact journal
Who wrote it: Jaehyuk Shim and 15 others · Seoul National University, Korea University, Institute for Basic Science (South Korea, Japan) · among the authors Taeghwan Hyeon, h-index 175
CONTEXTThe most compact electrolysers work in acid and need iridium, a very rare and expensive metal. Cheaper cobalt-based materials exist, but they dissolve in acid.
WHAT THEY DOThey add small amounts of other metals (antimony, germanium, indium or gallium) to a cobalt oxide; these bind to the cobalt and stop it dissolving.
RESULTIn a single electrolyser cell at 80 °C, the antimony version reaches more than 3,500 mA per cm² at 2.0 V and runs for more than 1,000 hours at 250 mA per cm².
WHY IT MATTERSRemoving iridium is one of the conditions for making green hydrogen cheap and available at large scale.
Hybrid renewable energy systemsgrowing
Research share +39% in 3 years · 4,474 papers in 2025
What it is about. Combines solar, wind, storage and hydrogen. Green hydrogen, made with renewable electricity, is meant for industries hard to electrify, such as steel and fertilisers.
The green hydrogen implementation gap: China's manufacturing-led dominance, Western policy asymmetries, and a socio-technical roadmap for global sustainability
Transactions in Energy and Sustainability · 24 October  Journal
Who wrote it: Alberto A. Boretti · h-index 48
WHAT THEY DOUsing International Energy Agency data and a review of the literature, the author compares how much green hydrogen is actually produced in different countries and why.
RESULTAs of 2025 China has about 74% of the world's operating green hydrogen capacity; the US, Germany, the UK, France, Spain, Australia and Canada together have less than 11%. Western announced projects are 50 to 130 times larger than what actually operates.
WHY IT MATTERSThe author argues that China leads by building electrolysers at industrial scale, not by better technology, which questions where Western policy puts its money.
Smart grid energy managementstable
Research share flat in 3 years · 3,214 papers in 2025
What it is about. Large batteries connected to the grid buy electricity when it is cheap and sell it when it is expensive, also helping to balance the grid.
Towards proactive control of grid-scale battery energy storage using dynamic preview length
Journal of Energy Storage · 25 October  Journal  High-impact journal  Free PDF ↗
Who wrote it: Shakil Mirza and 3 others · The University of Queensland (Australia), University of Cambridge (United Kingdom) · among the authors Tapan Kumar Saha, h-index 66
WHAT THEY DOA control system for community batteries that looks further ahead at forecast prices when the market is calm, and less when it is volatile, updating decisions every five minutes.
RESULTOver a full year, battery revenue rises by 9.23% compared with the usual fixed approach, with less computing effort.
WHY IT MATTERSHigher revenue makes shared neighbourhood batteries easier to pay for, and with them more solar power that can be used in the evening.
Photovoltaic system optimisationstable
Research share −4% in 3 years · 3,284 papers in 2025
What it is about. Small solar panels hung on a balcony and plugged into the home are spreading in Europe. With a small battery, the energy produced during the day can be used in the evening.
Monitoring the Performance of a Balcony-Mounted Photovoltaic System with Battery Storage in Northern Italy
Preprints.org · 23 October  Preprint – not peer reviewed  Free PDF ↗
Who wrote it: Stefano Rampino and 3 others · among the authors Antonino Laudani (University of Catania), h-index 31
WHAT THEY DOA full year of measurements on a balcony system near Parma: 1.38 kW of panels and a 2.56 kWh battery, set up so that no energy is sent to the grid.
RESULTThe system covers 32.3% of the home's needs over the year (55.8% in summer); 16.4% of the possible production is lost because it cannot be sent to the grid. In deep winter the inverter's standby consumption exceeds what the panels produce. The cost of about €1,100 pays back in 4.6 years.
WHY IT MATTERSReal data on a product many families are considering, including a winter trap that is easy to avoid. Not yet peer reviewed.
RADAR OF THE DAY · ENERGY
What it is about. How we produce, store and move energy: solar, wind, batteries, hydrogen, power grids and electric vehicles. It is the largest of the five verticals and the one most supported by public funding.

(year on year)
«battery»▲ +239%▼ −10%
«smart grid»▲ +184%▼ −44%
«solar energy»▲ +120%▼ −27%
«hydrogen»▼ −47%■ −3%
GitHub: new projects; Hacker News: stories discussed (only 9 to 33 per quarter for smart grid, hydrogen and solar). Q3 2026 vs Q3 2025; for comparison, all new GitHub projects grew 62% and Hacker News discussions fell 38%. Wikipedia, 12 months: views down for energy storage (−26%), hydrogen economy (−37%), perovskite solar cells (−30%), fusion power (−11%). Data updated 27 October.
In short: Developers pour into batteries and smart grids well beyond the average, while hydrogen is the only signal shrinking, in line with today's hydrogen paper. In research, energy holds steady but slows this year.
WORDS OF THE DAY
h-index — a measure of how often a researcher is cited: an h-index of 50 means 50 papers cited at least 50 times each. Above 40 usually indicates an established name in the field.
Cathode — the battery electrode that largely sets how much energy it can store; in phones and cars it is usually made of nickel, cobalt, manganese or iron compounds.
Electrolyser — a machine that splits water into hydrogen and oxygen using electricity, a bit like a battery working in reverse.
Green hydrogen — hydrogen made with renewable electricity, so without CO2 emissions; today most hydrogen is still made from natural gas.
WORTH WATCHING
Tomorrow the radar of the day is on LLMs and generative AI. Worth watching: if cobalt-free nickel cathodes hold up in larger cells, they could reach electric cars within a few years.
